title: Costco (COST) vs. Walmart (WMT): Which Retailing Giant Has a Wider Moat?
detail:
Costco (COST) vs. Walmart (WMT): Which Retailing Giant Has a Wider Moat?
Sanmit Amin

WMT
SPY

Costco Wholesale Corporation (NASDAQ:COST) and Walmart Inc. (NASDAQ:WMT) have returned -0.71% and -5.38%, respectively, during the last six months, as of October 15. This compares to a 21.5% return for the Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and 15.74% for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust.

Costco and Walmart have been ahead of the competition for a while, but both retail giants have different ways to go about it. Costco gets customers to keep coming back through its membership model, low prices, and popular Kirkland Signature brand. Walmart has a different opportunity. It can use its huge customer base and store network to grow its online business, advertising, and third-party marketplace. These businesses could help Walmart make more money from each sale over time. Costco, however, has already shown that its model works, with customers renewing their memberships and continuing to spend more.

JCostco (COST) vs. Walmart (WMT): Which Retailing Giant Has a Wider Moat?

Niloo / Shutterstock.com

Costco's Advantage Is Visible in Its Numbers

Costco generated $303.2 billion in revenue in fiscal 2026, including $5.9 billion from membership fees. Net income rose a solid 14% from the previous year to $9.2 billion, while comparable sales grew 6.6%, excluding gas and foreign exchange effects. The company ended the year with 84.1 million paid members, and its renewal rate in the US and Canada stood at 92.3%. The numbers suggest that Costco is getting more out of its existing members while continuing to bring in new ones.

The retailing giant's membership fees help it keep prices low, and Kirkland Signature gives customers another reason to shop there. The brand offers products that are often cheaper than national brands without giving up much on quality.

CHECK OUT: 10 Most Promising Technology Stocks to Buy Right Now

Costco's limited SKU strategy of stock enables it to purchase larger quantities of each item and thus secure better deals from suppliers. While other retailers are able to match its prices on a number of products, it is much more difficult for them to match both its buying power and the customer loyalty that Costco has developed over the years.

That said, Costco still has to work to keep growing. Membership growth is slowing. Membership income rose 7.3% in Q4, compared with 13.6% in Q2 and 10.7% in Q3. Also, opening new warehouses requires significant investment. The company needs these stores to generate good returns without losing sight of what keeps existing members coming back. Digital sales grew about 21% in fiscal 2026, giving Costco another avenue for growth. But the business ultimately comes down to whether members continue to see enough value to renew their memberships and spend more.

title: FTC mails $9.8 million to 65,000 Walmart wire transfer customers — here's how to check if you're owed a refund

FTC mails $9.8 million to 65,000 Walmart wire transfer customers — here's how to check if you're owed a refund
Eric Esposito
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 2:15 AM MST 5 min read
WMT
Trade Walmart on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Pat Greenhouse/The Boston Globe via Getty Images

Anyone who used Walmart's money transfer services might notice a check from the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) in their mailbox.

These refunds are part of a nearly $10-million settlement Walmart [NASDAQ:WMT] paid the FTC in 2025 over wire transfer fraud allegations. Back in 2022, the FTC sued Walmart over what it alleged were major security failures that allowed employees to process "tens of millions of dollars in fraud-related wire transfers annually for many years."

According to the FTC's claims, Walmart knew scammers were using its stores to collect money from victims of fraud schemes, but it didn't take enough action to warn customers and spot red flags. Allegedly, Walmart stores didn't put enough warning labels on forms, and employees weren't well-trained in proper fraud prevention.

In an October press release, the FTC said it just sent $9.8 million in 65,022 refund checks to Walmart customers who used eligible money transfer services between January 2015 and December 2024. Anyone who gets one of these checks should cash it within 90 days.

Regarding the 2025 settlement, a Walmart spokesperson told Moneywise, "We're pleased to have this matter behind us. While it is clear in the agreement that we do not admit fault, we share in the FTC's goal to protect consumers from fraudsters and continue to be dedicated to safeguarding consumers from fraud-induced money transfers."

Wire wiser: How to outsmart scammers

​The appeal of wire transfers is obvious. Since they send money directly between individuals or bank accounts, they're a very fast transfer method. Unfortunately, the FTC notes that this convenience comes with a safety trade-off that scammers love.

​The FTC's Director for the Bureau of Consumer Protection, Christopher Mufarrige, pointed out this vulnerability when talking about the $10-million Walmart settlement, saying, "Electronic money transfers are one of the most common ways that scammers tell consumers to send them money, because once it's sent, it's gone for good."​

Unlike other payment methods like credit cards, a wire transfer can make cash available immediately without a dispute period. By the time victims realize they've been duped, fraudsters have likely already withdrawn the funds and moved them to other accounts, making them harder to trace and recover.

Walmart (WMT) stock trades at 42.5 times earnings. Among the six retailers in its peer group, only Costco Wholesale is priced higher. Walmart ranks lower on business performance than on price. Over the latest four fiscal quarters, Walmart sits third out of six on revenue growth and fourth on operating margin. So how does Walmart's price look beside the rival that grows fastest?

Walmart Trades At Twice Amazon's P/E With Slower Growth

Amazon.com is the fastest grower in the group. It trades at 20.2 times earnings. Net income exceeded operating income at Amazon, meaning items outside its operations added to the earnings behind that P/E. Amazon revenue rose 15.8% over its latest four fiscal quarters, compared with 6.2% at Walmart. Amazon also posted an operating margin of 12.1%, well above the 4.4% at Walmart. Amazon is a broadline retailer, and Walmart is a consumer staples merchant. The two margins come from different kinds of business.

Costco operates in Walmart's own industry. It is priced higher at 47.1 times earnings. Costco's revenue also grew faster than Walmart's, rising 10.1%. Target and Home Depot are priced below Walmart and grew more slowly. Walmart maintains a price near the top of the group, while its growth sits in the middle and its margin sits in the lower half.

What Are You Buying At Walmart's Price?

Investors buying Walmart at this price are mostly buying its home market. The Walmart U.S. segment brought in $486 billion of the company's $713 billion revenue in fiscal 2026. The retailer sells at such high volume that a small change in margin represents a lot of money. In fiscal Q2 2027, with sales of $188 billion, each percentage point of margin is worth about $1.9 billion of operating profit.

Walmart is finding its faster growth in businesses built around those sales. The global advertising business grew 38% in fiscal Q2 2027. Walmart's membership fee revenue rose 17%. Management said almost half of Walmart's profit growth came from areas such as membership, advertising and marketplace, a trend the company expects to continue. The current share price appears to assume Walmart keeps growing these businesses fast enough to lift its margin.

title: How Benefit Expansion At Walmart (WMT) Has Changed Its Investment Story

How Benefit Expansion At Walmart (WMT) Has Changed Its Investment Story
Sasha Jovanovic
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 1:13 PM MST 4 min read
WMT
Trade Walmart on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

In October 2026, Deutsche Bank upgraded Walmart after the retailer expanded employee healthcare benefits, including more than 250 free prescription drugs and up to 12 weeks of paid NICU leave, while highlighting growth in higher margin areas such as advertising, marketplace services, and membership income.

The combination of richer worker benefits and a heavier mix of fee based businesses points to Walmart leaning on people and higher margin profit pools rather than pure price cuts to reinforce its value pitch during an inflationary period.

We will look at how Walmart's investment narrative is affected by richer employee healthcare benefits that support its higher margin businesses.

Capitalize on Walmart's value and services playbook by scanning a curated list of 33 high quality undervalued stocks that also lean on higher margin profit pools rather than pure price cuts.

Walmart Investment Narrative Recap

To own Walmart, you need to believe the retail giant can keep shifting its mix toward higher margin businesses like advertising, marketplace services, Walmart Fulfillment Services and Walmart+ membership, while holding onto its price appeal in a tough inflation backdrop. The key near term swing factor is whether e-commerce and ultra fast delivery stay profit accretive rather than returning to subsidised growth.

The biggest risk is rising cost and regulatory pressure around logistics, digital tools and healthcare commitments that could offset margin gains from those fee based profit pools. Recent news on richer employee benefits supports execution in higher service areas but does not materially change that central catalyst or the margin risk around unprofitable baskets.

The most relevant fresh announcement for this story is Walmart opening its fifth next generation fulfillment center in Stockton, California. That facility is heavily automated, designed to cut steps in order processing and supports both first party items and Walmart Marketplace sellers through Walmart Fulfillment Services, tying directly into the higher margin ecosystem analysts focus on.

This build out matters for investors watching whether Walmart can balance rapid delivery with the risk that small orders remain uneconomic. More efficient fulfillment, if executed well, can relieve some margin pressure from grocery delivery and support marketplace growth, while any operational hiccups or cost overruns would lean the other way and keep that core risk front of mind.

Walmart's current analyst narrative points to revenues of US$839.4b and earnings of US$29.5b by 2029, based on an assumed 4.5% yearly revenue growth rate and an earnings increase of about US$7.4b from current earnings of US$22.1b.

title: Home Depot vs. Walmart: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
detail:
Home Depot vs. Walmart: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
Mike Schwenk, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 9:20 AM MST 8 min read
WMT
Trade Walmart on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Deciding between Home Depot (NYSE:HD) and Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT) comes down to weighing a possible pickup in housing-related spending against Walmart's steadier growth in everyday essentials.

While both companies serve as anchors for American consumers, they operate at opposite ends of the retail spectrum. Home Depot focuses on projects for homeowners and professionals, and Walmart sells a broad range of essentials and discretionary goods in 19 countries.

The case for Home Depot

Home Depot serves two customer groups, do-it-yourself (DIY) homeowners and professionals (Pros) such as remodelers and general contractors. The company operated 2,359 stores at the end of fiscal 2025, according to its annual report. It has also expanded into specialty distribution.

Home Depot acquired SRS, a specialty trade distribution company, in fiscal 2024, and SRS completed the acquisition of GMS, a distributor of drywall and other construction products, in fiscal 2025. Home Depot says SRS had more than 1,340 locations at the end of the second quarter of fiscal 2026.

In the fiscal year ended Feb. 1, 2026, revenue reached approximately $164.7 billion, a 3.2% increase from the prior fiscal year that included an extra week worth about $2.5 billion in sales.

Reported net income for the same period was nearly $14.2 billion, down about 4.4% from the roughly $14.8 billion earned in the previous year. Adjusted diluted earnings per share fell about 3.6% to $14.69 from $15.24, according to the company's release.

As of its Feb. 1, 2026, balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio reached nearly 5.1x, counting both borrowings and lease obligations against shareholder equity. That indicates the company uses significant leverage. By the end of the second quarter on Aug. 2, 2026, the same ratio had eased to about 3.8x as equity rose and total debt fell by nearly $3 billion.

The current ratio, a measure of assets available to cover short-term obligations, was approximately 1.1x at fiscal year-end. For fiscal 2025, the company generated nearly $12.6 billion in free cash flow, defined as operating cash flow minus capital expenditures.

In the second quarter of fiscal 2026, which ended Aug. 2, 2026, sales rose 5.7% to $47.9 billion and comparable sales rose 1.7%, according to the company's Aug. 18 earnings release.

Home Depot reaffirmed its fiscal 2026 guidance, which calls for total sales growth of approximately 2.5% to 4.5% and comparable sales growth of approximately flat to 2%. It expects diluted earnings per share to grow approximately flat to 4% from $14.23 in fiscal 2025.

title: What the Latest Fed Decision Means for Costco, Walmart, Target, and Home Depot
detail:
What the Latest Fed Decision Means for Costco, Walmart, Target, and Home Depot
Ben Gran, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 6:14 AM MST 7 min read
WMT
TGT
COST
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

When interest rates go up, that tends to be bad news for stocks. But not all stocks are affected the same way by rising rates. At their most recent meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on Sept. 16, the central bankers hiked the benchmark federal funds rate by 0.25 percentage points. Inflation in September came in slightly hotter than expected, with a year-over-year CPI increase of 3.7%. That suggests that the Fed might hike rates again in 2026, as the FOMC will meet two more times this year, on Oct. 28 and Dec. 9.

When the Fed hikes interest rates, its goal is often to slow inflation -- and tap the brakes on economic growth. This can have negative effects on job growth, borrowing costs, and consumer spending. Some retail stocks might suffer more from a consumer spending slowdown than others. A few important retail stocks to watch right now are Costco (NASDAQ: COST), Home Depot (NYSE: HD), Target (NYSE: TGT), and Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT).

Here's how these four retail stocks have performed since the federal funds rate hike on Sept. 16:

COST Total Return Level data by YCharts.

A 25-basis-point rate hike is unlikely to be a game changer for any stock. But some companies are more rate-sensitive than others. All four of these retailers have distinct strengths and vulnerabilities that would come into play in a rising interest-rate environment.

Let's look at which of these retail stocks are more likely to be winners if the Fed hikes interest rates again in 2026, and which might be losers.

Image source: Getty Images.
Costco: Affluent consumers unfazed by higher gas prices

Costco might be better positioned than most retailers to thrive in an environment of higher inflation and rising interest rates. That's because Costco's membership model creates a high level of customer loyalty, and the retailer tends to be popular with higher-income customers. According to a June YouGov survey, 11% of Americans in households with gross incomes of $150,000 or more do most of their food and other grocery shopping at Costco. These more affluent households are likely to be less bothered by high inflation.

A major factor in the Fed hiking interest rates is inflation driven by higher gas prices. The latest CPI index for gasoline was up 9.1% year over year in September 2026. Higher gas prices could hurt some retailers more than others, as consumers are compelled to dedicate more of their take-home pay to filling their tanks.
